title: A method for assessing chemically-induced paralysis in headless mosquito larvae
author: Islam, Bloomquist

steps.title: Prepare larvae and saline solution
steps.instruction: Obtain early‑stage (1st or 2nd instar) Aedes aegypti larvae from USDA‑ARS, keep them in unfiltered tap water at ~25 °C and feed with a mixture of 3 parts liver powder (MP Biomedical) and 2 parts Brewer’s yeast (MP Biomedical). Use fourth‑instar larvae for all experiments. Remove heads by pressing the neck against a Sylgard (RTV 615A/B, General Electric Corp.) surface in a 35 mm dish (Becton Dickinson Labware) using one pair of forceps to hold the larva and a second pair to pull the head away while keeping the larva in a minimal amount of liquid. Transfer each headless larva (n = 10) to a small glass chamber containing 1 mL of mosquito larval physiological saline (NaCl 0.9 %, CaCl₂ 0.02 %, KCl 0.02 %, NaHCO₃ 0.01 %, pH 6.9). Test the saline pH before each use; all saline components are from commercial suppliers.

substeps.instruction: Obtain larvae and maintain at ~25 °C in tap water.
Feed larvae with 3 parts liver powder + 2 parts Brewer’s yeast.
Select fourth‑instar larvae for the assay.
Remove heads on Sylgard surface in a 35 mm dish using two pairs of forceps, minimizing liquid.
Place each headless larva (10 per experiment) into a glass chamber with 1 mL saline of specified composition.
Verify saline pH (6.9) before use.

steps.title: Set up microscopy and probing
steps.instruction: Place the glass chamber under a standard dissecting microscope (World Precision Instruments, Model PZMT111) equipped with a video camera (Model DFK 31AU03, The Imaging Source) and computer interface. Observe each headless larva and elicit a response by gently probing it with an insect pin.

substeps.instruction: Arrange microscope and connect video camera.
Position the chamber containing the headless larvae under the microscope.
Probe each larva with an insect pin to stimulate movement.

steps.title: Classify larval behavioral response
steps.instruction: Based on the reaction to probing, categorize each larva as: (1) Active – rapid bilateral abdominal contractions; (2) Sluggish – attenuated response but not paralyzed; (3) Paralyzed/Dead – no movement after probing. For drug‑effect quantitation, treat Active and Sluggish larvae as unaffected.

substeps.instruction: Observe the larva after probing.
If rapid bilateral contractions occur, label as Active.
If response is weak but movement occurs, label as Sluggish.
If no movement occurs, label as Paralyzed/Dead.

steps.title: Expose larvae to test compound
steps.instruction: Prepare stock solutions of the experimental compound (e.g., l‑aspartate) in the same physiological saline. Add the appropriate volume of stock to the saline bath containing the headless larvae to reach the desired test concentration (e.g., 10 ppm). Monitor larval motility for at least 5 h (the period during which >90 % of untreated headless larvae remain active) and record the type and timing of paralysis. Note that l‑aspartate produced a flaccid paralysis with a PC₅₀ of 4.2 ppm (95 % CL 1.3–13.0 ppm) at 5 h; 10 ppm caused complete paralysis within 4 h, while 1000 ppm had no effect on intact larvae over 24 h.

substeps.instruction: Make a saline‑based stock solution of the test compound.
Add stock to the larval bath to achieve the target concentration.
Observe and record larval motility for ≥5 h.
Note paralysis type (spastic vs. flaccid) and time to onset.

steps.title: Quantify larval movement post‑probe
steps.instruction: After probing each larva with an insect pin, count the number of distinct movements performed within a 3‑second interval. Perform this count at defined time points (e.g., hourly). Untreated headless larvae typically show ~2.5 movements per 3 s at 5 h, whereas larvae exposed to 10 ppm l‑aspartate show ~2.2 movements in the first hour, decreasing to zero by the fifth hour.

substeps.instruction: Probe the larva with an insect pin.
Count movements occurring during the subsequent 3 s.
Record the count at each scheduled time point.
Compare counts to control values to assess impairment.
